passage: I'm Vinita from next door, and I've been dropping in on Hafsa most evenings this month. Every evening I watch her son Zayan, nine, redo his homework three or four times because one letter leans. Hafsa sits beside him looking proud and worried at once; she bites her lip, then smiles when he gets it right. Last night he cried over a rubbed-out map. Hafsa didn't say, "Stop being silly." She said, "You care about doing it properly. I love that. But look, yesterday I burnt the rice, and we still ate." He laughed a little. Then she said, "Good enough is fine for homework." I can't tell what he thought, but he closed the book.

qa.q: How old is Zayan?
qa.a: He is nine.

qa.q: What does Hafsa's bitten lip suggest while she watches Zayan?
qa.a: It suggests she feels proud and worried at once about how hard he pushes himself.

qa.q: Which of Hafsa's choices helped Zayan most, and why?
qa.a: She praised his care, shared that she had burnt the rice and said good enough is fine, without shaming his high standards.

qa.q: How might Zayan feel hearing that his mother burnt the rice?
qa.a: He may feel relieved and less alone, which is why he laughs a little.

grounding: A neighbour watches a mother torn between pride and worry at her son's perfectionism, who shares her own mistake and says good enough is fine.

passage:
Monday: Uday found Mehak, ten, still at her desk at ten at night, redrawing a science diagram because one arrow was "too thick". He felt a rush of pride at her care, then a knot of worry. "Beta, it's fine," he said. She burst into tears.
Wednesday: He tried something else. At dinner he told her about the document he'd sent at work with a typo on page one. "My boss laughed. I fixed it. The office is still standing." Mehak giggled.
Saturday: While drawing a card for Dadi, Mehak smudged the corner. She froze, then looked at Uday. "Good enough?" she asked. "Good enough," he said. She drew a flower over the smudge.

qa.q: Why was Mehak redrawing the diagram?
qa.a: Because one arrow was "too thick".

qa.q: What did Uday feel on Monday night, and why?
qa.a: He felt proud of her care but also worried, seeing her still at her desk so late over one arrow.

qa.q: What turning point on Wednesday changed things?
qa.a: Uday shared his own typo at work, showing mistakes can be fixed, which made Mehak giggle and relax.

qa.q: How might Mehak feel asking "Good enough?" on Saturday?
qa.a: She may feel nervous but braver, checking that it's safe to leave a small flaw.

grounding: Over a week, Uday, torn between pride and worry, shares his own mistake, and Mehak begins to accept good enough.

passage: At the parent-teacher meeting in the school hall, Kishore listened as the class teacher praised his son Anand's neat notebooks, top marks and perfect attendance. Kishore felt the old swell of pride. Then she added quietly, "He cried in class on Monday because he wrote one answer in the wrong box. He wouldn't stop until I let him redo the whole page." Kishore's pride turned into a knot. On the way to the car, Anand walked a step behind, silent. Kishore stopped under the neem tree. "You know, at my first job I sent a letter to the wrong company. My boss laughed, and I fixed it. I was fine." Anand looked up. "You never told me that." "Your high standards are great. Mistakes are allowed too."

qa.q: Why did Anand cry in class on Monday?
qa.a: He wrote one answer in the wrong box.

qa.q: What did Kishore feel during the meeting?
qa.a: He felt torn: proud of Anand's work, then worried when he heard about the crying.

qa.q: Which choice of Kishore's was wise, and why?
qa.a: Sharing his own work mistake without shaming Anand's standards, which showed that errors can be fixed.

qa.q: How might Anand feel hearing about the wrong letter?
qa.a: Anand is likely surprised and a little relieved to learn his father made mistakes too.

grounding: Shows a parent torn between pride and worry about a perfectionist child, sharing his own mistake without shaming high standards.

passage:
Monday: Vijay tore up his maths worksheet because one sum had a crossing-out, and sobbed at the dining table. Charu felt proud of how much he cared, and scared by how hard he cried.
Wednesday: While frying puris, Charu burnt the first batch. "Oops, burnt them all," she said, laughing. "First batch is always practice." Vijay stared at her.
Saturday: Vijay handed her his English homework with one word scratched out. "It's good enough," he said, sounding unsure. Charu didn't praise the neatness. She said, "I like how you kept going." He smiled a little.

qa.q: What did Charu burn on Wednesday?
qa.a: The first batch of puris.

qa.q: What did Charu feel on Monday when Vijay tore up the worksheet?
qa.a: She felt proud of how much he cared and scared by how hard he cried.

qa.q: What worked in how Charu helped Vijay over the week?
qa.a: She laughed at her own mistake and praised his effort rather than neatness, showing that good enough is fine.

qa.q: How might Vijay feel handing over homework with a scratch-out?
qa.a: Vijay seems nervous and unsure, but also braver, trying out "good enough".

grounding: Shows over a week a parent torn between pride and worry who models her own mistakes and praises effort.

passage: Ojas, you get this from your father, you know. When Mohit was nine, he'd rewrite a whole essay if one letter leaned. I was so proud of his neat books, and so worried when he cried at midnight over a smudge. One night I did something I'd never done. I, Jyoti, showed him my old college file, full of red marks, and told him about the exam I failed and passed the next year. He couldn't believe his mother had ever failed. After that, when he fretted, I'd say, "Good enough is good enough, beta. Now sleep." I never told him to stop caring. Just to stop hurting. Now look at him. He still double-checks everything, but he sleeps.

qa.q: What did Jyoti show Mohit?
qa.a: Her old college file, full of red marks.

qa.q: What was Jyoti feeling about young Mohit's habits?
qa.a: She was proud of his neat books and worried when he cried at midnight over a smudge.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story?
qa.a: Jyoti sharing her own failed exam, which showed Mohit that mistakes can be survived.

qa.q: How might young Mohit have felt seeing his mother's red marks?
qa.a: Mohit was probably amazed and relieved, learning that even his mother had failed and recovered.

grounding: Shows a parent torn between pride and worry who shares her own failures and teaches good enough without shaming standards.

passage:
The school bus would come at 7:20, and at 7:05 Yash was still repainting one corner of his volcano model. "The brown is uneven! I can't take it like this."
Hemant looked at the clock, then at his son's shaking hands. Part of him was proud; Yash worked so carefully. Part of him ached.
"Yash, look at me." He crouched down. "Remember my office presentation last month? I spelled the company's name wrong on the first slide. Big letters."
Yash stared. "What happened?"
"Someone pointed it out, I said oops, and we carried on. They still gave us the project."
Yash sniffed.
"Your volcano is good enough. The uneven corner is fine, I promise. And I love how much you care."
At 7:18, they carried it out together, one corner a little uneven.

qa.q: What time was the school bus coming?
What was Hemant feeling as he watched Yash repaint the corner?
qa.a: He felt torn: proud of how carefully Yash worked, but also worried and aching to see him so stressed.

qa.q: What did Hemant do well to ease Yash's stress?
qa.a: He shared his own spelling mistake and how it turned out fine, and said the volcano was good enough without shaming Yash's care.

qa.q: What would change if Hemant had said "Stop being silly"?
qa.a: Yash might feel ashamed of caring so much, and his stress could get worse instead of easing.

grounding: Shows a father torn between pride and worry at his son's stress over tiny errors, sharing his own mistake and showing good enough is fine.
